home.hero_desc: An open-source project mapping automatic licence plate readers (ALPRs) across Canada.
home.body1: An automatic licence plate reader (ALPR or LPR) is an AI-powered camera that photographs {vehicle} and logs the details — the plate, the location, and the exact time. Many also capture a car's {details}, plus {features} like dents, roof racks, or bumper stickers, turning each vehicle into a set of {datapoints}.
home.body2: Every plate gets recorded, {suspected}. Marketed as essential crime-fighting tools, these cameras instead build a running log of where ordinary people go — {investigation}.
home.body2_suspected: whether or not the driver is suspected of anything
home.demo_caption: Example of an annotated licence plate reader photo showing captured vehicle details
home.privacy_body: ALPRs {track} and {store} for long periods of time, creating a detailed record of {history}
home.misuse_body: Mass surveillance data has repeatedly been misused — for profiling, tracking individuals, and access by officers for personal reasons, often with little oversight.
home.benefits_body: There's {evidence} that blanket ALPR surveillance meaningfully prevents crime, despite vendors' marketing claims.
home.risk_body: ALPRs are a serious risk to your privacy and civil liberties. These systems {warrant}, probable cause, or even reasonable suspicion. Your driving history is {confined} to the town or city where the cameras are installed — it is often shared with many other agencies, and in some cases {crossborder}. Once the data leaves your community, you have little control over how it's used.
home.risk_warrant: continuously record your movements without a warrant
home.risk_crossborder: across the border with U.S. law enforcement
home.vendors_body: In Canada, the most commonly mapped ALPR systems come from {genetec}, a Montréal-based company, alongside {flock} — a major U.S. vendor now expanding into Canada. Captured vehicle data is uploaded to the vendor's cloud system, where participating agencies can {share}.
home.vendors_share: search and share information across jurisdictions
home.vendors_other: These are {notonly}, and others follow similar practices. See this list of {link}.

learn.video_caption: Video explanation of modern LPRs by Christophe
learn.p1: An automatic licence plate reader (ALPR, sometimes LPR) is an AI-driven camera that captures an image of {everyvehicle} and stores what it sees — the plate number, the place, and the precise time. Many models also note a car's {makemodelcolour}, and even identifying marks such as dents, roof racks, or bumper stickers, converting each one into {searchabledata}.
learn.p2: These cameras log millions of vehicles {nosuspicion}. Sold as indispensable tools against crime, they instead record the {everyday}, with little judicial oversight over how the data is kept or searched.
learn.p2_nosuspicion: regardless of whether anyone is under suspicion
learn.p3: For more on how ALPRs threaten privacy, see resources from Canadian groups like the {ccla} and {openmedia}, along with the {eff} and {aclu}.
learn.concern_intro: ALPRs erode privacy and chip away at civil liberties. Here's how:
learn.us_note: Many of the documented cases below come from the United States, where ALPR surveillance is most entrenched — but the same vendors and systems (Flock, Genetec, Motorola) are now expanding across Canada.

dangers.crime_p1: There's no independent research proving that ALPRs can reduce crime. Headlines and supporting studies claiming otherwise are often produced by the companies selling ALPRs and the police agencies buying them.
dangers.crime_p2: For example, Flock Safety claims that {flockclaim} The study that Flock cites was conducted by two Flock employees and “given legitimacy with the ‘oversight’ of two academic researchers whose names are also on the paper” according to {report404}. Flock Safety is using the veneer of an academic study as part of its sales pitch.
dangers.crime_p2_flockclaim: 10% of Reported Crime in the U.S. Is Solved Using Flock Technology.
dangers.crime_p3: What research does exist regarding the ability of ALPRs to reduce crime is inconclusive at best:
dangers.crime_quote1: Our findings indicate that, when small numbers of LPR patrols are used in crime hot spots in the way we have tested them here, they do not seem to generate either a general or offense-specific deterrent effect.
dangers.crime_quote2: There is not even a moderate degree of correlation between ALPRs and stolen vehicle recoveries, let alone any apparent casualty
dangers.crime_quote2_attr: Automated Licence Plate Readers: A Study in Failure
dangers.security_title: ALPRs Are a Major Security Risk
dangers.security_p1: Companies that make ALPRs have a history of poor security practices, which can lead to data breaches and unauthorized access to sensitive information. For example:
dangers.security_li1: In November 2025, {link}, since Flock negligently doesn't require multi-factor authentication, an alleged violation of industry-standard security practices.
dangers.security_li1_link: a security researcher found Flock logins for sale on Russian hacking forums
dangers.security_li2: In January 2025, Motorola Solutions' ALPR system was {link} that allowed anyone to access live data from their cameras. Data includes {data}. A {livefeed} of both cameras (color and infrared) was also available to stream using a web browser.
dangers.security_li2_link: found to have a critical security flaw
dangers.security_li2_data: licence plate numbers, make, model, colour, and timestamps
dangers.security_li3: In July 2025, {link} that included (1) their internal search interface and some source code, some of which reveals how they calculate confidence scores for vehicle tracking and (2) a live ArcGIS admin API key, which included access to over 50 private data layers.
dangers.security_li3_link: Flock Safety exposed a misconfigured demo site
dangers.dragnet_p2: A study of ALPRs in Piedmont, CA, found that {percent} of ALPR hits might translate into a useful investigative lead. Most licence plates recorded were not on a hot list, yet police still logged information on people's movements throughout the day.
dangers.dragnet_p3: Flock Safety provides Transparency Portals to their police customers, which allow the public to see the data collected by ALPRs. These portals reveal that the vast majority of licence plates scanned are not on a hot list (vehicles suspected of being involved in crimes). For example:
dangers.abuse_p1: There are many documented cases where police have knowingly used ALPRs to commit crimes and put people in danger. These examples illustrate that it can be difficult to put meaningful restrictions in place that prevent ALPRs from being used for nefarious purposes. It's often only after harm is done that an officer is caught and punished, if at all.
dangers.abuse_li1: Texas police used Flock ALPRs to track a woman who had an abortion across state lines
dangers.abuse_li2: A police officer used Flock Safety ALPRs to stalk his estranged wife in Kechi, KS
dangers.abuse_li3: A police officer accepted a bribe to run a woman's licence plate in Georgia
dangers.abuse_li4: A police officer used ALPRs to stalk his ex-girlfriend in Ohio
dangers.abuse_li5: California agencies keeping data longer than necessary and sharing it with unauthorized agencies
dangers.abuse_li6: Police in San Diego County breaking the law sharing drivers' data
dangers.encounters_title: ALPR Usage Leads to Dangerous Police Encounters
dangers.encounters_p1: The negligent use of ALPRs has led to dangerous police encounters, including pulling guns on innocent drivers. Here are just a few examples:
dangers.encounters_li1: San Francisco Woman Pulled Out of Car at Gunpoint Because of Licence Plate Reader Error
dangers.encounters_li2: Cops Terrorize Black Family but Blame Licence Plate Reader for Misidentifying 'Stolen' Vehicle
dangers.encounters_li3: Deputies Sued After False ALPR Hit Leads To Guns-Out Traffic Stop Of California Privacy Activist
dangers.encounters_li4: Privacy advocate sues CoCo sheriff's deputies after licence plate readers target his car stolen
dangers.encounters_li5: {link} after incompetent detectives relied on Flock cameras to pin a {'$'}25 package theft on her {video}.
dangers.encounters_li5_link: A Denver woman had to prove her innocence
dangers.racist_p1: ALPRs are more likely to surveil communities with a higher density of Black and brown people, reinforcing systemic racism in policing.
dangers.racist_p2: The Electronic Frontier Foundation {link} and found that ALPR cameras were more likely to scan licence plates in communities with a higher density of Black and brown people than in communities with a higher density of white people.
dangers.racist_p2_link: reviewed the use of ALPRs by the Oakland Police Department
dangers.racist_p3: {link} shows that after 9/11, the NYPD used ALPRs to monitor Muslims visiting mosques.
dangers.racist_p3_link: A report by The Associated Press
dangers.racist_p4: A study of Flock Safety's impact in Oak Park, IL found:
dangers.racist_quote: In the first 10 months of their use, 84% of the drivers stopped by Oak Park police because of Flock were Black.
dangers.crossborder_p1: ALPR data doesn't stay local. In the U.S., the same Flock network now expanding into Canada has been tapped by federal immigration agencies (ICE), often even where local policy prohibits it. As Canadian agencies adopt these systems, the risk that Canadians' movement data is shared across the border with U.S. agencies is a serious concern:
dangers.crossborder_li1: ICE Taps Into Flock's Nationwide Camera Network, Data Shows
dangers.crossborder_li2: Police in Pasadena, Long Beach pledged not to send licence plate data to ICE. They shared it anyway.
dangers.crossborder_li3: Documents Reveal ICE Using Driver Location Data From Local Police for Deportations
dangers.crossborder_li4: New report finds data sharing with federal immigration agencies might violate Washington law

about.p1: panopti.ca is an open-source project that maps the spread of automatic licence plate readers (ALPRs) across Canada. Its purpose is to make a quiet form of mass surveillance visible — to show where these cameras stand, who runs them, and just how widely they have been deployed.
about.p2: An ALPR is an AI-powered camera that photographs and logs {vehicle} — its plate, its location, and the moment it drove by — whether or not the driver is suspected of anything. Sold by vendors such as {genetec} and {flock}, these cameras are spreading rapidly through Canadian cities and towns, often with little public debate or oversight.
about.p3: Surveillance that nobody can see is hard to question. Plotting each known camera on a public map turns scattered, easily-overlooked deployments into something concrete — something residents, journalists, and elected officials can examine, discuss, and challenge. A map also makes the scale of the problem legible in a way that a single camera on a pole never could.
about.p4: Every camera location lives on {osm}, the same open dataset that powers maps around the world. Nothing sits in a private database: the information is public, verifiable, and free for anyone to inspect, correct, or reuse. The project builds on the open-source work of {deflock}, which pioneered crowdsourced ALPR mapping in the United States.
about.p5: The map grows through the people who use it. Spotting a camera and {adding} puts it on the map for everyone, and sharing the site helps more people understand how ALPR surveillance works and where it is taking hold. Guidance on {learn} and how to identify and report them is available throughout the site — no special expertise required.

faq.necessary_q: Are ALPRs a necessary tool for police?
faq.necessary_a: No. Police have long had ways to obtain location information about suspects. Those methods generally require reasonable grounds and judicial authorization, which provide oversight and accountability. In Canada, {section8} protects against unreasonable search and seizure. ALPRs flip this around: they collect location data on {everyone}, all the time, and that data is often searched with little or no oversight.
faq.necessary_a_section8: Section 8 of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms
faq.nothingtohide_q: Why should I care if I have nothing to hide?
faq.nothingtohide_h1: 1. You don't get to decide what looks suspicious tomorrow.
faq.nothingtohide_p1: Just because you're not doing anything wrong today doesn't mean you won't be watched tomorrow. Licence plate cameras like Flock don't know your intentions—only your movements. A trip to a protest, a place of worship, a union meeting, a friend's house in a “high-crime” area, or even a misread plate can flag you as “suspicious.”
faq.nothingtohide_p2: History shows that when governments or third parties gain unchecked surveillance powers, those powers are eventually turned on people who weren't doing anything wrong—{until}. Tools built for one purpose are routinely repurposed for another.
faq.nothingtohide_h2: 2. Mistakes happen, and you're the one who pays for them.
faq.nothingtohide_p3: Automated Licence Plate Readers (ALPRs) are not always accurate. People have been pulled over at gunpoint, arrested, or detained because a camera misread a plate or flagged the wrong car.
faq.nothingtohide_p4: If you “have nothing to hide,” you also have nothing to correct the record with when a machine error points the finger at you.
faq.onlycrimes_q: Do these cameras only record vehicles involved in crimes?
faq.onlycrimes_p1: {allvehicles}, not just those involved in crimes. They capture licence plates, unique identifying features, locations, dates, and times of every vehicle, regardless of whether the driver is suspected of wrongdoing. This means that even if you're not doing anything wrong, your movements are still being tracked and stored, often for long periods of time.
faq.onlycrimes_p1_allvehicles: No, ALPRs record all vehicles that pass by
faq.onlycrimes_p2: The data collected by ALPRs can also be shared with other agencies and third parties, further extending the reach of this surveillance. Most people have no idea their movements are being monitored and recorded.
faq.warrant_q: Do police need a warrant to search these cameras?
faq.warrant_p1: This is a serious and unsettled question in Canada. ALPRs collect data on {everyone}—not just suspects—and that data can often be searched with {oversight}. Mass, suspicionless tracking of Canadians' movements raises significant concerns under {section8}, which protects against unreasonable search and seizure.
faq.warrant_p2: Data is also frequently shared across agencies—and, in some cases, {crossborder}—extending the reach of this surveillance far beyond the community where the cameras were installed.
faq.warrant_p2_crossborder: across the border with U.S. law enforcement
faq.oversight_q: What oversight is there for these systems?
faq.oversight_p1: {lead} Some police services have policies governing ALPR use, but these are frequently weak and poorly enforced, and many agencies have no policy at all. There is rarely any requirement for transparency or accountability in how these systems are used.
faq.oversight_p1_lead: There is often little to no meaningful oversight.
faq.oversight_p2: Vendors like Flock offer a {portal} for their law-enforcement customers, but they let customers choose what to include or exclude, and the portals often {lackdata}—for example, underreporting how many agencies actually have access.
faq.transparency_q: Do Flock's transparency portals give a full picture of who has access to the data?
faq.transparency_p1: Flock now operates in Canada, but its track record in the United States—where it has operated longest—is telling. Flock's transparency portals are {incomplete} and often {misleading}. They let law-enforcement agencies cherry-pick what is included or excluded, leading to significant underreporting of who actually has access to the data.
faq.transparency_p2: Take Boulder, Colorado for example. Their {portal} listed around 90 agencies with access to their ALPR data. However, {request} revealed that {count} actually had access. This discrepancy highlights the lack of transparency and accountability in Flock's reporting.
faq.trust_q: Can Flock be trusted to keep this data safe?
faq.trust_p1: Flock's record raises serious doubts. In November 2025, {link}, since Flock negligently didn't require multi-factor authentication.
faq.trust_p1_link: a security researcher found Flock logins for sale on Russian hacking forums
faq.trust_p2: Flock has also been caught misrepresenting the facts. Its CEO told Denver's 9News that Flock had {nocontracts}—yet weeks later, {found} that U.S. Border Patrol did have access to search Flock's systems. Records requests later showed “U.S. Border Patrol” searching thousands of agencies' data across the national network.
faq.trust_p3: The same company is now signing up Canadian agencies—so these questions matter here too.
faq.remove_q: How can I get these cameras out of my city or town?
faq.remove_p1: Communities can push back. Raise concerns publicly, build a group of advocates, and petition your municipal council not to approve or renew ALPR contracts. Public attention, deputations, and records requests have led agencies elsewhere to cancel or decline ALPR programs.

report.hero_desc: Add or edit ALPRs using OSM's powerful web-based editor.
report.heading: Editing the Map
report.intro: Cameras are added through OpenStreetMap, the free and open map of the world. Pick what you're adding below — the steps are the same; only the tags in step 3 differ.
report.guided_alert_text: Prefer a guided tool? Sign in with OSM and add or edit cameras right on the map.
report.step1_body_signup: Sign up for an OpenStreetMap account
report.step2_body: {launch} and search for the location of the camera. You can use the search bar at the top of the page to find the location.
report.step3_intro: Once you've found the location of the camera, click the {edit} button in the top left corner of the page. This will open the OpenStreetMap editor, where you can add the ALPR to the map.
report.step3_warning: Add cameras as {standalone}! Do not connect them to roads, buildings, or other objects. Place the point exactly where the camera is physically located, but keep it as an independent point on the map.
report.step3_add_point: To add the camera, click the {point} button at the top center of the editor, then click on its location on the map. In the popup that appears, paste the tags below.
report.operator_alert: {tag1} is the key tag — it's what places the camera in panopti.ca's {layer} layer. Set {operator} to the city or agency that runs it. Optionally add {zone} for traffic cameras, or {mount} and {direction} if you know them.
report.step3_paste: After copying the tags, paste them into the {tags} field in the popup.
report.step4_body1: If you know the direction that the camera is facing, you can use the up and down arrows to set the direction it faces.
report.step4_body2: To report two cameras that are on the same pole, separate directions with a semi-colon ({semicolon}).
report.step5_intro: Optionally, you can add an image to your submission as well. If you choose to do this, {signup}
report.step5_intro_signup: you will need to sign up for a wikimedia commons account.
report.step5_wizard: Open the {wizard} after logging into your account. Make sure to read the graphic and confirm you understand the rules about what can be uploaded to wikimedia commons.
report.step5_upload: Upload your image of the ALPR and click {continue}.
report.step5_license: Make sure you publish the image under a {cc0} licence.
report.step5_title_caption: Give your image a descriptive title and caption so that other users understand what it is. For example, you could title the image {example}. Make sure the date is accurate. Optionally, you may add the image to a category or add a capture location if you wish.
report.step5_publish: After you're doing filling everything out, click {publish} at the bottom of the page.
report.step5_link_image: Finally, link your image on the point you created in OSM. Copy the title of your published image, including {file} and {jpg}. Create a new tag called {tagname} and paste your title as the value.
report.step6_body: Once you've added the camera to the map, click the {save} button in the top right corner of the editor. You'll be asked to provide a brief description of your changes. Once you've submitted your changes, the camera will be added to OpenStreetMap.
report.time_alert_body: We refresh data from OpenStreetMap {often}, so it may take up to a day for your changes to appear on this site. Rest assured that your changes will be reflected here soon.

council.hero_desc: Push back on ALPRs through the bodies that actually decide in Canada — your municipal council and your police services board.
council.intro_body: Local officials rely on hearing from residents. Here's how to push back on mass surveillance with the people who actually make these decisions.
council.who_subtitle: It's often the police services board, not just council
council.who_p1: In most Canadian cities, a municipal police service is overseen by a civilian {psb} (in Ontario, recently renamed a "police service board"). ALPR programs are frequently approved at the {boardword} level — and forces often acquire the technology by {piggyback} rather than running a public tender, which can mean very little public debate.{footnote}
council.who_p2: That gives you {twoplaces}: your {citycouncil} (which approves budgets and responds to public pressure) and your {psb} (which sets policy and oversees procurement). Find out which body is considering ALPRs in your community, and target both.
council.talking_body: Common questions, arguments & responses for discussing surveillance
council.step1_subtitle: Personal conversations are often the most effective approach
council.step1_body: Reach out to your {councillors} and {psbmembers} directly. A short, personal conversation helps them understand the human impact of surveillance before a vote.
council.step1_schedule_li1: Contact their office by phone or email
council.step1_schedule_li2: Suggest a coffee, a call, or their office
council.step1_schedule_li4: Mention you're a constituent concerned about ALPRs
council.step1_tips_li1: Bring a brief printed summary of key points
council.step1_tips_li2: Share local concerns about privacy and community impact
council.step1_tips_li3: Ask their position and listen to their concerns
council.step1_tips_li4: Follow up with answers to anything they raise
council.step1_email_body: Hello [Councillor / Board Member], I'm a [city] resident concerned about a proposed automatic licence plate reader (ALPR) program. Would you have 15 minutes to discuss it? I'd like to share some community concerns and hear your thoughts before it comes to a vote.
council.step2_subtitle: Register as a delegation to create an official record
council.step2_body: Most councils and police boards let residents speak as a {delegation} (sometimes called a deputation) for a few minutes. It puts your opposition on the public record and shows officials that people are watching the vote.
council.step2_before_li2: Register as a delegation in advance (often required)
council.step2_before_li4: Bring printed copies for the clerk
council.step2_during_li2: State your name and connection to the community
council.step2_during_li3: Lead with a clear local point
council.step2_during_li4: Stay respectful and thank them for their time
council.step2_tip: {protip} Focus on how ALPRs affect {your} community specifically — retention, data-sharing across the border, and the lack of oversight. Local, concrete points land harder than abstract arguments.
council.step3_subtitle: Freedom-of-information requests reveal what's really being approved
council.step3_body: Before a vote, file an access-to-information request for the {vendorcontract}, the {pia}, and the {retention} — including anything allowing {crossborder}. These documents often make the strongest case.
council.cta_body: Get in touch, and if you spot an ALPR, add it to the map so your community can see it.
council.footnote1: Police-board governance and piggyback procurement of ALPR are documented in Canadian municipal records (e.g., {ottawa}); see also {ipc}. Processes vary by province and municipality.

foi.hero_description: Use Canada's access-to-information laws to find out where ALPRs are and how they're used.
foi.why_p1: ALPRs are being installed across Canada with very little public transparency. A 2023 national survey found that {stat}, and most had no written procedure governing it.{ref} Access-to-information (FOI) requests let you find out where the cameras are, how long data is kept, who it's shared with, and what your local police agreed to when they signed up.
foi.why_p1_stat: 57% of responding police services use ALPR
foi.why_p2: Filing a request is something any resident can do, and the documents you get back help build a complete, public picture of these surveillance networks.
foi.law_intro: It depends on {who}. Canada's access regime is layered:
foi.law_municipal: {label} (most ALPRs) — your province's {foilaw}. In Ontario, the request goes to the {board} under MFIPPA (administered by the service's access & privacy unit).
foi.law_provincial: {label} (e.g., the OPP, SQ) — the {prov} FOI law (e.g., Ontario's FIPPA).
foi.law_federal: {label} — the federal {act} (ATIP): a {fee}, filed via the ATIP Online portal, by email, or by mail, with a {timeline} standard to respond.{ref}
foi.commissioners_intro: Each province and territory has its own access law and an independent privacy commissioner who handles appeals. The most common ones for ALPR records:
foi.commissioners_on: {label} — MFIPPA (municipal police) / FIPPA (OPP), overseen by the {link}.
foi.commissioners_on_link: Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario
foi.commissioners_bc: {label} — FIPPA, overseen by the {link} (public bodies have ~30 business days to respond).
foi.commissioners_qc_act: Act respecting access to documents held by public bodies
foi.commissioners_other: {label} (AB, SK, MB, NS, NB, NL, PE + territories) has its own FOI statute and commissioner — search "{search}" to find the portal.
foi.request_intro: Ontario's privacy commissioner says police using ALPR should make much of this public already,{ref} so these records exist and can be requested:
foi.request_li1: The {records} with the vendor (Flock Safety, Genetec, Motorola, etc.)
foi.request_li5: A {desc}: the number and type of camera vehicles and any {fixed}
foi.request_li6: Public-consultation records and the most recent {report}
foi.request_li6_report: annual ALPR report to the police board
foi.tip: {tiplabel} Address municipal-police requests to the {board} (the legal "institution"), even though the police service's access & privacy unit will process them. If you're unsure where records live, you can send the same request to more than one body.
foi.who_p: In most provinces, {anyone} can file — you generally don't need to be a resident, a lawyer, or explain why you want the records.
foi.cost_p: Federal ATIP requests have a {fee} application fee. Provincial/municipal fees vary (some have a small application fee, some none), and agencies may charge for search or copying time on large requests. You can ask for a fee estimate or a fee waiver.
foi.refused_heading: What if my request is refused?
foi.refused_p: Agencies can withhold some records (e.g., for law-enforcement or third-party reasons), but you can {appeal}. Commissioners have sided with the public before: in 2012 the BC commissioner found that retaining and sharing {nonhit} ALPR data served no law-enforcement purpose and wasn't authorized under FIPPA.{ref}
foi.refused_appeal: appeal or complain to your privacy commissioner
foi.found_p: If your records reveal where cameras are, {link} so everyone benefits.
foi.fn1: Pelletier, {journal} (2024) — survey of Canadian police services.
foi.fn3_link: IPC Ontario — Guidance on the use of ALPR by police (2024)
foi.disclaimer: This page is general information, not legal advice; details vary by province.

identify.hero_desc: Learn to identify LPRs and other devices
identify.feature2_body: Look for infrared lights that emit a {glow} at night.
identify.feature3_body: Many LPRs are powered by nearby {solar}.
identify.vendors_subheading: Most LPRs are easy to recognize.
identify.no_device_note: Don't see a device you know about? We're always adding more, so check back later!
